{{Short description|Rules used in ship stability and naval architecture}}
{{for|Simpson's rules used in numerical analysis|Simpson's rule}}

'''Simpson's rules''' are a set of rules used in ship stability and [[naval architecture]], to  calculate the [[area]]s and [[volumes]] of irregular figures.<ref name=derett>{{cite book|author1=Bryan Barass  |author2=D.R.Derett |title=Ship stability for Masters and Mates|publisher=Elsevier Butterworth|location=United Kingdom|page=69|url=http://seaworm.narod.ru/2/Stab1.pdf}}</ref>  This is an application of [[Simpson's rule]] for finding the values of an [[integral]], here interpreted as the area under a curve.

[[File:Simpsonrule1.jpg|thumbnail|right|Simpson's First Rule]]

== Simpson's 1st rule ==

Also known as the '''1–4–1 rule''' (after the multipliers used ).<ref>{{cite book|last=Rhodes|first=Martin|title=Ship Stability for Mates/Masters|year=2003|publisher=Seamanship International|location=United Kingdom|url=https://www.mandibooks.com|page=70}}</ref>

: <math> \text{Area} = \frac{h}{3}( a + 4b + c).</math>

== Simpson's 2nd rule ==
[[File:Simpson2rule.jpg|thumbnail|right|Simpson's Second Rule]]

Also known as the '''1–3–3–1''' rule, Simpson's second rule is a simplified version of [[Simpson Rule|Simpson's 3/8 rule]].<ref>{{cite book|last=Subramaniam|first=Capt. Harry|title=Nutshell series – Ship Stability III|publisher=Vijaya Publications|location=Mumbai, India|url=http://vijayabooks.com/book-list.php}}</ref>

: <math> \text{Area} = \frac{3h} 8 (a + 3b + 3c + d).</math>

== Simpson's 3rd rule ==

Also known as the '''5–8–1 rule''',<ref>{{cite book|last=Donkum, Enkhuizen|first=Van|title=ShipStability|publisher=Dokmar publications|isbn=978-90-71500-15-2|url=http://www.theartofdredging.com/dokmar.htm|year=2010}}</ref> SImpson's third rule is used to find the area between two consecutive ordinates when three consecutive ordinates are known.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bhange|first=Archana Ashish|date=February 2017|title=Simpson's Rules and {{as written|I|t's [sic]}} Application in Ship Stability|url=http://academicscience.co.in/admin/resources/project/paper/f201702151487147028.pdf|journal=International Journal of Computer & Mathematical Sciences|volume=6|pages=7|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180425053611if_/http://www.academicscience.co.in/admin/resources/project/paper/f201702151487147028.pdf|archive-date=25 April 2018}}</ref>

: <math>\text{Area} = \frac h {12} (5a + 8b - c ).</math>

This estimates the area in the left half of the figure for Simpson's 1st Rule while using all three pieces of data.

== Use of Simpsons rules ==
Simpson's rules are used to calculate the volume of [[lifeboat (shipboard)|lifeboat]]s,<ref>{{cite book|last=Kitching|first=Capt. R.C.E.|title=Introduction to Ship Stability|publisher=Starpath Publications|location=Canada|url=https://www.starpath.com/catalog/books/1712p.htm}}</ref> and by surveyors to calculate the volume of [[sludge]] in a ship's oil tanks. For instance, in the latter, Simpson's 3rd rule is used to find the volume between two co-ordinates. To calculate the entire area / volume, Simpson's first rule is used.<ref>{{cite book|author1=V.L. Belenky |author2=N.B Sevastianov|title=Stability and Safety of Ships|publisher=The Society of Naval Architects and Marine Engineers|location=USA|isbn=978-0-939773-61-9|url=https://www.sname.org/Pubs/Books/|year=2007}}</ref>

Simpson's rules are used by a ship's officers to check that the area under the ship's GZ curve complies with IMO stability criteria.
